"They're sacrificing quite a lot of revenue here," Waddell said . He estimated that fees add up to about a third of the average price for lawn seats. "It looks like it could be a really strong year," he said. "People want to go to shows. They want to hear music." Every tour offers some type of promotion, he said, including a lot of $10 lawn seats. "This is a business that's pretty flexible when it needs to be," he said. Live Nation began selling tickets to its own concerts only last year, just months before announcing plans to merge with Ticketmaster, the world's largest ticket-seller. Before that, Live Nation promoted shows but had no infrastructure to sell tickets, and it contracted out to Ticketmaster or others to sell them. The Ticketmaster-Live Nation merger plan has drawn criticism. The Justice Department launched an investigation of the proposed merger in February. Neither Live Nation nor Ticketmaster executives would respond to questions about the merger. However, Ticketmaster CEO Irving Azoff did talk about it before a U.S. Senate subcommittee earlier this year. The merger "will give us greater flexibility in how we promote, market and sell tickets to events," he said. "It will give us a pathway to alternative pricing and fee structures. And we will be better able to develop new and innovative products and services that enhance the fan experience and make all forms of entertainment more accessible to everyone." CNN's Denise Quan contributed to this report.

LOS ANGELES, California (CNN) — The additional service fees long tacked onto concert ticket prices—and long a source of frustration for ticket buyers—will disappear this summer for millions of seats sold by the largest U.S. concert promoter.

Live Nation, which is awaiting government approval of a merger with ticketing giant Ticketmaster, is launching “No Service Fee Wednesdays” this week for lawn seats at amphitheaters. The promotion will eliminate extra fees on 5 million lawn seats for shows at amphitheaters across the United States.

Live Nation insisted that the promotion is intended to sell more tickets and help music fans affected by difficult economic times—not to improve its public image while awaiting government approval of the Ticketmaster merger. Still, the move could help ease some public frustration.

“People get a little ticked off when they think they’re paying $20 for a ticket and as they progress along the various pages of the electronic transaction, they see more fees added along the way,” said Ray Waddell, who covers live music tours for Billboard magazine.

Live Nation will waive fees on lawn seats for 24 hours, beginning at midnight Tuesday local time and continuing through Wednesday.

Lawn-seat tickets available this week include concerts by Aerosmith, Blink-182, Coldplay, No Doubt, Nickelback, Depeche Mode, Toby Keith, Brad Paisley and many others, Live Nation said.

Other shows scheduled for later in the summer include Crosby, Stills & Nash; Crue Fest 2; Def Leppard with Poison and Cheap Trick; Jason Mraz; Kid Rock & Lynyrd Skynyrd; Incubus; New Kids on the Block; Nine Inch Nails and Jane’s Addiction; Phish; the Dead; Rascal Flatts with Darius Rucker; the Allman Brothers Band; the Fray; and the Killers.

“They’re sacrificing quite a lot of revenue here,” Waddell said. He estimated that fees account for about one-third of the average price of lawn seats.

The economic recession has not appeared to slow the live concert business, which, “considering everything else, is going like gangbusters,” he said.

“It looks like it could be a really strong year,” Waddell said. “People want to go to shows. They want to hear music.”

Every tour offers some type of promotion, he added, including many $10 lawn-seat offers.

“This is a business that’s pretty flexible when it needs to be,” he said.

Live Nation began selling tickets to its own concerts only last year, just months before announcing plans to merge with Ticketmaster, the world’s largest ticket seller. Previously, Live Nation promoted shows but lacked the infrastructure to sell tickets, contracting with Ticketmaster or other companies to handle sales.

The proposed Ticketmaster-Live Nation merger has drawn criticism, and the Justice Department opened an investigation into the plan in February.

Executives from both Live Nation and Ticketmaster declined to respond to questions about the merger. However, Ticketmaster CEO Irving Azoff addressed the matter before a U.S. Senate subcommittee earlier this year.

The merger “will give us greater flexibility in how we promote, market and sell tickets to events,” Azoff said. “It will give us a pathway to alternative pricing and fee structures. And we will be better able to develop new and innovative products and services that enhance the fan experience and make all forms of entertainment more accessible to everyone.”

CNN’s Denise Quan contributed to this report.

LOS ANGELES, California (CNN) — For millions of concertgoers this summer, the added service charges that have long irritated ticket buyers will be eliminated on seats sold by the largest concert promoter in the United States.

Live Nation, which is waiting for federal approval of its proposed merger with ticketing giant Ticketmaster, is beginning a promotion this week called “No Service Fee Wednesdays.” The offer applies to lawn seats at amphitheaters and removes additional fees from 5 million such tickets for shows around the country.

The company said the effort is intended to boost ticket sales and assist music fans struggling during difficult economic times, not to improve its image while regulators review the Ticketmaster deal. Still, the move may help ease some public frustration.

Ray Waddell, who covers concert touring for Billboard magazine, said customers often become annoyed when they believe a ticket costs $20, only to see extra charges appear as they move through each step of an online purchase.

Live Nation will drop the fees on lawn seats for a 24-hour period, starting at midnight Tuesday local time and continuing through Wednesday.

Tickets included in this week’s offer cover performances by Aerosmith, Blink-182, Coldplay, No Doubt, Nickelback, Depeche Mode, Toby Keith, Brad Paisley and numerous other acts, according to Live Nation.

Additional concerts scheduled later in the summer include Crosby Stills & Nash, Crue Fest 2, Def Leppard with Poison and Cheap Trick, Jason Mraz, Kid Rock & Lynyrd Skynyrd, Incubus, New Kids on the Block, Nine Inch Nails and Jane’s Addiction, Phish, the Dead, Rascal Flatts with Darius Rucker, the Allman Brothers Band, the Fray and the Killers.

Waddell said Live Nation is giving up a significant amount of money through the promotion. He estimated that service fees can make up roughly one-third of the typical lawn-seat price.

Despite the recession, the live concert industry has not appeared to lose momentum, Waddell said, describing it as performing extremely well “considering everything else.” He added that the year could turn out to be very strong because audiences still want to attend concerts and hear live music.

He also noted that nearly every tour uses some kind of promotion, including many offering $10 lawn seats. The concert business, he said, can adjust quickly when necessary.

Live Nation only started selling tickets for its own shows last year, a few months before announcing its plan to combine with Ticketmaster, the world’s biggest ticket seller. Previously, Live Nation promoted concerts but did not have its own ticket-selling system, so it relied on Ticketmaster or other companies to handle sales.

The proposed Live Nation-Ticketmaster merger has faced criticism. In February, the U.S. Justice Department opened an investigation into the deal.

Executives from both Live Nation and Ticketmaster declined to answer questions about the merger. However, Ticketmaster CEO Irving Azoff discussed it earlier this year before a U.S. Senate subcommittee.

Azoff said the merger would provide more flexibility in promoting, marketing and selling event tickets. He also said it would create opportunities for different pricing and fee models, while allowing the company to develop new products and services designed to improve the fan experience and make entertainment more widely available.

CNN’s Denise Quan contributed to this report.

That is why a promotion like “No Service Fee Wednesdays” carries significance beyond short-term savings. It gives Live Nation a chance to demonstrate that it can lower costs for fans, even as consumer advocates question whether a larger combined company would have enough incentive to do so in the long run.

For fans, the practical impact depends on the show. On lower-priced lawn seats or mid-tier tickets, eliminating service fees can make a noticeable difference. For families or groups buying multiple seats, the savings can add up quickly. But fee-free promotions typically apply only during limited windows and may exclude certain events, premium seats or non-Live Nation shows.

Still, the move reflects a broader shift in the concert business. Promoters have increasingly used discounts, bundled offers, lawn-pass deals and limited-time sales to fill venues and appeal to fans who may be reluctant to commit at full price. As touring costs rise and consumer budgets remain under pressure, pricing strategy has become as important as the lineup itself.

Waddell and other industry experts have pointed out that live music remains a powerful draw, but fans are more selective than ever. A major superstar tour may still sell out quickly, while mid-level tours and large amphitheater packages may need aggressive marketing or special offers to drive attendance.

“No Service Fee Wednesdays” does not end the debate over ticket fees, nor does it resolve the questions surrounding Live Nation’s proposed merger with Ticketmaster. But it does highlight a central tension in the live entertainment business: fans want transparency and affordability, while promoters, venues, artists and ticketing companies all rely on a complex system of revenue streams.

For now, Live Nation is betting that removing fees — even temporarily — will encourage fans to click “buy” and head back to the concert lawn. Whether that helps ease broader concerns about the company’s growing influence in the ticketing world remains a much larger question.
